lessons.title: Draw your first connection
lessons.goal: Build a source block and connect its result to a register.
prerequisites: Install and build UarchDraw using the course setup instructions.

steps.title: Draw one block
learn: Create a plain-text file named work.uarch. Paste this complete source into it.
uarch 2 selects the authoring language; title names the drawing.
block source gives the component a stable ID. label changes the displayed name. Braces contain declarations for this block.
observe: One rectangle named Source appears under the default DESIGN stage.
There are no ports or wires yet.

steps.title: Give the block an output
learn: Keep the block and add out data: bits(32) inside its braces.
out declares a driver port; data is its local ID; bits(32) declares a 32-bit scalar.
The tool chooses the right edge for this data output. You have not specified coordinates.
observe: The rectangle gains an output anchor and the port name data.
An output does not need a receiver. There is still no wire.

steps.title: Connect a result register
learn: Append a second block and a connect statement after the source block.
register(32) is a built-in interface with input d and output q. The colon selects the symbol/interface constructor.
source.data and capture.d identify block ports. The arrow declares one driver and one receiving input.
Inputs must be driven unless explicitly optional; declaring capture and its connection together keeps this checkpoint valid.
observe: Source is on the left and Result register is on the right.
A labeled 32-bit wire ends with an arrow at the receiving d port.
The register q port has no wire yet; drawing a register does not simulate its clocked behavior.

exercise.task: Rename the displayed Source to Operand source without changing its block ID or connection.
explanation: Change only label. source.data still identifies the driver.
The block grows to fit the longer display name; connectivity stays at one net and one sink.

reviewQuestions: How does changing a display label differ from changing a block ID?
Which declaration creates the output port, and which declaration creates the wire?

lessons.title: Types, parameters and fanout
lessons.goal: Change one width parameter and give one driver multiple receivers.
prerequisites: Complete lesson 01. Start from its connected source and register.

steps.title: Make the width a parameter
learn: Insert param W = 16 before the declarations that use W. Replace both hard-coded widths with W.
A parameter is a named integer used during expansion. Both ends still have exactly the same type.
Default wire labels follow the driver type, so /16 now appears without editing a label.
observe: The topology is unchanged: two blocks and one wire.
The wire width annotation changes from /32 to /16.

steps.title: Add a second receiver
learn: Add Observer and its required sample input, then append another connect from source.data.
Separate connect statements from the same driver merge into one net. Do not invent another output to represent the branch.
A junction dot marks a connected branch. A crossing without that dot is not a connection.
observe: One source reaches both the register and Observer.
There is one named net with two receiving ports, rather than two independent driver nets.

exercise.task: Change the whole fanout diagram to 64 bits by editing only the parameter.
explanation: All three ports use W. One parameter edit updates every endpoint and the automatic /64 annotation.

errors.title: Mismatch one receiver width
explanation: Observer now expects 8 bits, while Source still drives 16 bits.
Fix the receiver to bits(W). Editing the visible wire label cannot repair a type mismatch.

reviewQuestions: Why must every receiving port have the same type as its driver?
Why does the fanout checkpoint contain one net even though it reaches two inputs?

lessons.title: Select an ALU operand
lessons.goal: Add a MUX, its control input and a distinct ALU symbol.
prerequisites: Complete lesson 02. This lesson starts a new operand-selection diagram.

steps.title: Build a two-input selector
learn: Replace work.uarch with this complete source; this is a new diagram, not an append to lesson 02.
stages declares the architectural left-to-right sequence. in INPUT assigns a block to a stage.
mux(2, W) creates d[0], d[1], select and out. Square brackets address one element of its data-port array.
bit means bits(1). Choice produces the required one-bit select input. role control describes its lane; style control makes its net dashed.
Connection options use braces. label overrides display text but does not change signal type.
observe: Two data wires enter the tapered MUX at input 0 and input 1.
A dashed control wire enters select; the selected data reaches Capture.
All four nets have visible names; /16 is a display convention, and the actual width comes from the ports.

steps.title: Put an ALU after the selector
learn: Insert EXECUTE between SELECT and CAPTURE. Add a custom alu block with explicit a, b and result ports.
Replace the old MUX-to-register connection with MUX-to-ALU and ALU-to-register connections.
Append the connection from operands.a to compute.a with the same explicit label as its existing fanout net.
The alu symbol has two operand edges and a central input notch. Naming a block ALU alone would not select this shape.
observe: ALU appears between the MUX and Capture.
A now branches to MUX input 0 and ALU input a. Selected enters ALU input b.
The figure describes connectivity; it does not evaluate select values or ALU arithmetic.

exercise.task: Change the visible names A/16 and B/16 to Primary/16 and Alternate/16 without swapping their destinations.
explanation: Only labels change. operands.a still drives d[0], and operands.b still drives d[1].
To change topology you would edit the destinations, not the visible names.

errors.title: Remove the MUX control connection
explanation: The MUX still has a required select input. Restore its connect statement.
UarchDraw rejects a missing electrical connection instead of drawing an apparently complete selector.

reviewQuestions: Which MUX port is control, and how does it look different from the data wires?
Trace what reaches ALU a, ALU b and the result register in the final checkpoint.

lessons.title: Scale with port arrays
lessons.goal: Grow a selector by changing parameters instead of repeating declarations.
prerequisites: Complete lesson 03. Replace its separate operand declarations with a sample array.

steps.title: Select four samples
learn: out data[N] creates N output ports. The ${index} display substitution numbers the ports from zero.
[*] connects corresponding elements of two equally sized arrays. This one statement expands four data nets.
clog2(N) computes the select width, with a minimum of one bit. Four inputs need two select bits.
The comma-separated destinations fan out Channel to both the MUX select input and Capture tag.
Bare register selects the shape while the body supplies a custom sample/tag interface; it does not add built-in d/q ports.
observe: Four named horizontal channel wires enter a 4:1 MUX.
Channel/2 controls selection and also tags the captured sample.
There are six nets: four channels, one index fanout and one selected sample.

steps.title: Grow to eight samples
learn: Change only param N = 4 to param N = 8. Keep the port and connect declarations unchanged.
The array expands, the MUX grows, and INDEX_W becomes three. ${index} and ${W} labels are recomputed.
observe: The MUX becomes 8:1, with eight data wires and a /3 channel index.
All sample wires remain horizontal; no row, span or alignment edits are needed.

steps.title: Grow to sixteen samples
learn: Change N to 16 and render again. A taller canvas is the cost of showing every input clearly.
Read the SVG at a useful zoom rather than judging legibility from a small page thumbnail.
observe: The MUX becomes 16:1 with inputs 0 through 15, and the index width is /4.
All sixteen channel labels remain visible and data paths stay horizontal.

exercise.task: Generate eight 64-bit samples by editing only N and W.
explanation: Set N to 8 and W to 64. The select index remains three bits; sample width becomes 64 bits.

errors.title: Connect arrays with different lengths
explanation: Samples has four elements but the MUX now has five. Wildcard pairing requires equal lengths.
Restore mux(N, W); the compiler will not silently drop or repeat an element.

reviewQuestions: Which two parameters control channel count and sample width?
Why does N = 16 need four index bits, and why must wildcard arrays have equal lengths?

lessons.title: Reuse interfaces with templates
lessons.goal: Refactor repeated port declarations without changing the circuit.
prerequisites: Complete lesson 04. Start from its four-input checkpoint.

steps.title: Extract the Samples interface
learn: Replace the Samples block body with a template definition and an instance of that template.
COUNT and WIDTH are local template parameter names. Samples(N, W) binds the argument values to them.
The template supplies ports and presentation; it does not instantiate internal subcircuits.
Keep all connections unchanged: source IDs still belong to the samples instance.
observe: The same four channel paths and six nets remain.
This step improves reuse rather than adding hardware. Compare port names and destinations with lesson 04.

steps.title: Extract a register interface
learn: Replace the custom Capture block with a TaggedCapture template.
The : register on the template chooses the symbol kind. DATA_W and TAG_W bind locally for each instance.
Instance IDs still define connectivity. A reusable template name does not appear in port references.
observe: Capture keeps its sample and tag inputs and its register shape.
The drawing remains a four-input selector; the interface definition is now reusable.

exercise.task: Instantiate the same output template at widths 8 and 32, and connect each instance to a matching receiver.
explanation: Output(8) and Output(32) bind independent local WIDTH values.
Each receiver has the matching type. Reusing the template does not force all instances to one width.

reviewQuestions: Which names belong to a template, and which belong to a block instance?
Why can the same Output template produce both an 8-bit and a 32-bit interface?

lessons.title: Bundles, feedback and a FIFO
lessons.goal: Name bundle fields, route a return signal, then add a ready/valid datapath.
prerequisites: Complete lessons 02 and 05. This lesson starts a new storage/control diagram.

steps.title: Send a typed status bundle
learn: type Flags declares a structural bundle with named full and empty fields. Each field is one bit.
Both ports use Flags. Equal total width alone would not make a different set of field names compatible.
role data keeps Storage in the main lane even though its only current net is status. Handshake is a control block.
Open the generated .signals.md file to read the bundle fields; the diagram shows one whole-bundle wire.
observe: Storage sends one dashed status{2} bundle to Handshake.
The {2} annotation denotes the total bundle width; it does not mean an array with two elements.

steps.title: Return push and pop commands
learn: Declare Commands with push and pop fields. Add an input on Storage and an output on Handshake.
The return connection points from the later CONTROL stage back to STORAGE. corridor bottom prefers a lower return channel.
A cycle in the connectivity diagram is valid. Signal directions still distinguish the unique driver from each receiver.
observe: Two distinct bundle wires connect the blocks in opposite directions.
status carries full/empty toward Handshake; commands carries push/pop toward Storage.
These declarations document a contract; they do not calculate or execute push/pop.

steps.title: Add the data and ready/valid interfaces
learn: Keep Flags and Commands, then add the Producer(W) and Consumer(W) templates from this complete checkpoint.
Storage gains data/head ports. Handshake gains valid/ready and out_valid/out_ready ports.
Connect data from Producer through Storage to Consumer. The four scalar control connections describe the two handshakes.
Restore all connections before rendering: every new input is required. The final contract uses ready = !full and out_valid = !empty.
observe: The upper path carries Producer data through FIFO storage to Consumer.
Handshake sits below it. Status and commands join storage/control; ready returns toward Producer and from Consumer.
Eight named nets remain individually traceable. The figure does not verify FIFO pointer logic or capacity.

exercise.task: Make the complete FIFO datapath 64 bits while keeping its flags and commands unchanged.
explanation: Only W changes. Producer, Storage and Consumer data widths become 64.
Flags and Commands remain two-bit bundles with their original field names.

errors.title: Change a bundle field while retaining its total width
explanation: Flags and OtherFlags both total two bits, but full and occupied are different field names.
Restore the receiving port to Flags. Structural bundle checks preserve the intended interface meaning.

reviewQuestions: Why are two bundles with the same total width sometimes incompatible?
Trace status, commands and both ready signals in their actual driver-to-receiver directions.

lessons.title: Derive hierarchy views
lessons.goal: Generate full, overview and detail drawings from one connectivity model.
prerequisites: Complete lessons 01 and 05. This lesson starts a small processing chain.

steps.title: Build the complete chain
learn: Create four blocks and three connections. Compute is a generic block here, not an ALU constructor.
Keep the architectural stages explicit so source, execution and output remain ordered.
observe: Four rectangles form a chain with three labeled data nets.
Compute and Result register are separate components in EXECUTE.

steps.title: Put execution blocks in nested groups
learn: Wrap Compute and Result register in group execute, then wrap that group in group core.
Inside execute, compute.result and latch.d are local references. Outside, use core.execute.compute.operand and core.execute.latch.q.
Group labels describe views. They do not add electrical ports or change the expanded graph.
Keep the external source and consumer outside core so the group has real boundary connections.
observe: The ordinary render still shows four components and three nets.
The grouping changes organization without adding or removing hardware from the full graph.

steps.title: Collapse the core for an overview
learn: Keep the same grouped source. Add --overview to the render command below.
The tool collapses top-level core and derives its boundary ports from the existing nets.
This is a view of the same model; do not hand-author a second disconnected overview diagram.
observe: Processing core replaces Compute and Result register.
Source and Consumer remain visible, with two original boundary nets and their 32-bit types.

steps.title: Focus on the nested execute group
learn: Keep the same source and render with --focus core.execute.
The dotted path selects a nested group. The resulting view adds context blocks for real external drivers and receivers.
Boundary nets retain their IDs and types; the detail view does not create substitute signals.
observe: Compute and Result register are visible again.
Operand source (external) and Result consumer (external) explain where data enters and leaves the group.
The detail has three nets, including the internal compute-to-register connection.

exercise.task: Rename the displayed Processing core to Integer core, then render an overview without renaming its group ID.
explanation: Change the label inside group core. The group ID and qualified port paths remain unchanged.
Render with --overview to see Integer core as the collapsed block.

reviewQuestions: Which internal net disappears from the overview, and which boundary nets remain?
Why do external context blocks appear in the focus view?

lessons.title: Spacing and deliberate layout hints
lessons.goal: Observe automatic spacing recovery and make one explicit placement change.
prerequisites: Complete lessons 01 and 07. Return to a two-block diagram to isolate layout effects.

steps.title: Start with automatic placement
learn: Use no layout section and no @side overrides. The engine measures the symbols and places the blocks.
Keep this small baseline so the next edit changes only one display label.
Open the .planning.json companion file to see the number of attempts and effective spacing.
Capture uses the custom register form from lesson 04. Its D and Q display labels are explicit, so they remain visible when placement becomes fixed. The electrical port IDs stay d and q.
observe: One horizontal wire labeled Data/32 connects two blocks.
The short label fits the initial spacing profile.

steps.title: Let the planner make room for a long name
learn: Change only the connection label. Keep its driver, receiver and type unchanged.
When the name no longer fits, the compiler measures it and retries with a wider gap.
The planner tries at most four spacing profiles. This is bounded recovery, not a promise that every graph can be routed.
observe: The two blocks move farther apart and the full label remains visible.
The console reports expanded spacing; .planning.json records more than one attempt.
Compare the topology with the preceding checkpoint: it is still one 32-bit net.

steps.title: Move the receiver to another row
learn: Return to the short Data/32 label, then add a layout section inside Capture.
Specify both column and row to fix this block. Column is local to its stage; row is the shared vertical grid index.
Automatic peers remain automatic. A layout hint changes presentation, not electrical identity.
observe: Capture appears lower and the data wire bends to reach it.
There are still two components and one net.
Use hints only when the automatic result needs a deliberate architectural emphasis.

exercise.task: Move Capture one more row down without editing the connection.
explanation: Set row to 2 and keep column 0. The receiver moves farther down, so the route gets longer.
The source and destination port IDs remain unchanged.

errors.title: Disable spacing recovery for the long-label source
explanation: Run the same long-label checkpoint with --no-adaptive. Initial spacing is insufficient.
Remove --no-adaptive to restore the verified result. A failed check writes no output files.

reviewQuestions: Which file reports that spacing expanded, and what does --no-adaptive change?
Does moving Capture to row 2 change its electrical source?

lessons.title: Build an automatic arbiter
lessons.goal: Combine arrays, templates, control lanes and feedback in a common datapath.
prerequisites: Complete lessons 03–08. Start from the scalable selector rather than the full CPU diagram.

steps.title: Start with five queue heads
learn: Start from the templated selector in lesson 05. Set N to 5 and W to 32.
This checkpoint still gets its index from Channel; it does not yet show requests, grants or output backpressure.
observe: Five parallel 32-bit inputs enter a 5:1 MUX.
The three-bit index also reaches Capture tag.

steps.title: Add arbitration and output backpressure
learn: Replace the Samples interface with Queues: retain its data array and add request and grant vectors of N bits.
Replace Channel with Round-robin: request enters it, grant returns to Queues, and index drives the MUX.
Add Any request. The same request net fans out to both controllers; its valid output drives Output buffer valid.
Replace tagged Capture with the buffer/consumer interfaces shown below. Connect buffer data and out_valid forward, consumer.ready back, and buffer.ready to arbiter.accept.
Read these new connections in that order before rendering. Controllers declare role control; all physical coordinates and alignments remain automatic.
observe: The five data paths stay above the controllers and lead through Output buffer to Consumer.
Request, grant, select, valid and ready are individually named dashed signals.
The diagram has six blocks and fourteen nets. The behavioral contract advances priority only when the buffer accepts data; the compiler does not prove fairness.

steps.title: Add a sixth queue with one edit
learn: Change N from 5 to 6. Keep the templates, wildcard connections and layout unchanged.
Request and grant vectors grow to six bits. The select index stays three bits because clog2(6) is three.
observe: A sixth horizontal data wire appears and the MUX becomes 6:1.
The design now has fifteen nets; the control structure remains recognizable.

exercise.task: Generate a sixteen-input arbiter without adding port, net or placement statements.
explanation: Set N to 16. The data array, request/grant vectors and MUX expand together.
The select index becomes four bits. Open SVG and zoom to inspect the taller figure.

reviewQuestions: Which signal returns to the arbiter when the output buffer can accept data?
What changes when N becomes 6, and which declarations stay exactly the same?
